content.title: What is the International Space Station? | Teaching Wiki
content.text: Learn all about the International Space Station, how the ISS was built and the astronauts that live and work on the ISS in our informative Teaching Wiki.What is the International Space Station? The International Space Station (ISS) is a large spacecraft in low Earth orbit. It is an artificial satellite, which means it is an object made by humans that orbits Earth. Almost as large as a football pitch, the ISS is the largest artificial object in space and is a home for astronauts who sometimes stay there for many months. It weighs almost 400,000 kg (400 tonnes). The ISS is also a science laboratory circling the Earth because astronauts conduct lots of scientific experiments on board. The ISS is a great place to conduct science experiments because astronauts experience microgravity on board the ISS. In microgravity, objects appear to be weightless because the force of gravity is weaker than on Earth. Astronauts from many countries all over the world have travelled to the ISS. The ISS is a large international collaboration that has brought many countries together, even countries that have political tensions on Earth, such as America and Russia. 16 countries worked together to build the ISS. There have been campaigns for the ISS to win a Nobel Peace Prize. It is the biggest worldwide cooperation in science and technology in human history. The ISS project is possible due to a partnership between five space agencies from around the world: Europe (ESA: European Space Agency) America (NASA: National Aeronautics and Space Administration) Japan (JAXA) Canada (CSA) Russia (Ruscosmos) At an orbit height of 400 km above Earth, we can often see the ISS from Earth. The ISS travels at 28,800 km/hour around the Earth. It only takes the ISS 92 minutes to complete a full orbit of Earth, so in one day the ISS orbits the Earth 16 times. This means that astronauts on board the ISS experience 16 sunrises and sunsets each day! How was the International Space Station built? The ISS was assembled in space, piece-by-piece. There is no rocket big or powerful enough to launch the entire ISS into space in one go, so it could not be built on Earth and launched into space. Instead, it was gradually built in orbit around Earth. It took more than 40 missions for the ISS to be put together and over 221 spacewalks have taken place to assemble and maintain the ISS. The first piece was launched into space in 1998 and the final part was added in 2011. Humans have lived continuously on the ISS for 19 years, with the first humans arriving in 2000. A big central truss makes up the largest part of the ISS with 16 big solar panels attached. The astronauts live and work in modules attached to the centre of the truss. If you line up all of the solar panels next to each other, they are as big as eight basketball courts. The solar panels constantly rotate to catch as much sunlight as possible to power the ISS. Inside, the ISS is as big as a jumbo jet! It needs to be so large to accommodate all the science experiments and equipment the astronauts need, as well as places for them to sleep, exercise and work. There are 52 computers controlling the ISS and up to six astronauts can live on board the ISS at one time. As well as manned spacecraft missions to deliver people and equipment to the ISS, there are some uncrewed spacecraft (with no astronauts on board) called Automated Transfer Vehicles (ATVs). These spacecraft deliver food, fuel, equipment and other supplies to the ISS. Even though air and water is recycled on board the ISS, around seven tonnes (7000 kg) of supplies are needed to support three astronauts for six months on board the ISS. The ISS is the most expensive object ever built! It is estimated to have cost around $120 billion. Components of the ISS were manufactured all over the world, then shipped to the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida for the last stages of manufacturing and machine assembly. The first humans on the International Space Station Expedition 1 carried the first three humans to the ISS in the year 2000. The station was made up of only three different modules: the Zarya Module (power control module), Unity Module (used for docking with the space station) and Zvezda Service Module. The Zvezda Service Module was the most important module for providing living quarters, life support systems, electrical power distribution, data processing, flight control systems and propulsion systems. It would not have been possible for life to survive in space without this module. The Expedition 1 crew stayed for four months in the ISS. When they first arrived, they set up the sleeping quarters, performed communication checks and activated the food warmer. Since then, almost 250 astronauts from 19 different countries have been to the ISS! Astronauts have to do two hours of exercise a day on the ISS to make up for the loss of muscle and bone mass in the human body due to being in space. Science experiments on the International Space Station One of the main laboratories on board the ISS is ESA’s Columbus Lab, which is one of the leading labs for scientific research. More than 2,700 experiments have been conducted in the Columbus lab, with over 108 different countries sending experiments up to the ISS. There can be up to 250 different experiments happening simultaneously. The crew also act as living experiments themselves, with bone scans and eye examinations showing the effect that living in space can have on the human body. Some interesting experiments on board the ISS have been: An identical twin study. One of the twins flew to the ISS and one stayed on Earth. NASA monitored the changes that spaceflight causes to the human body by studying the different between the two twins. Scott Kelly, one of the brothers, spent nearly a year on board the ISS, which caused shifts in his gene expression compared to his brother Mark. Discovering a new state of matter. A new state of matter, different to solids, liquids, gases and plasmas, was created on board the ISS. It is called a Bose-Einstein condensate. Studying Alzheimer’s. There are lots of experiments related to human health happening on board the ISS, including studies into diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Observing plants in space. Astronauts have been able to grow vegetables like lettuces on board the ISS, which has helped them improve their diets when they are in space for a long time.
